Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify the anatomic structures that act as stabilizers to the elbow joint.
Describe the Horii circle and the sequence of soft-tissue disruption in a simple elbow
dislocation.
Recognize the common patterns of elbow instability, including valgus instability, posterolateral
rotator instability, and varus posteromedial instability.
Determine the appropriate rehabilitation protocol for specific elbow dislocations.
Apply the surgical indications and basic procedures for the management of acute and chronic
elbow instability.

Overview

The elbow is the second most commonly dislocated joint in adults and the most commonly
dislocated joint in children.
Dislocations represent 10% to 25% of all elbow injuries.
Recurrent instability results from ligamentous, bony, or combined injuries.

Overview
Elbow dislocations are a relatively common injury, occurring at a rate of 5.21 dislocations
per 100,000 person-years.1 Elbow dislocations are classified as simple or complex.
Simple dislocations are not associated with bony injury, whereas complex dislocations
are associated with a fracture. Simple dislocations are more common and tend to
respond to nonsurgical management.2 Dislocations associated with osseous avulsions,
which are not thought to affect stability, also are classified as simple dislocations.
Epidemiology
The highest incidence of elbow dislocation is in patients aged 10 to 20 years.
Most commonly occur with a fall on an outstretched hand
Dislocations are commonly associated with athletics.

Epidemiology
Dislocations most commonly occur in adolescents, with males having a slightly higher
risk than females; 44.5% of dislocations are associated with athletics.1 The mechanism of
injury is most commonly a fall onto an outstretched hand. Males have a propensity to
dislocate during contact sports, such as football, wrestling, and basketball.1 Females
most commonly dislocate during gymnastics and skating sports.1 Although less
common, dislocations occur in adults and often are associated with osseous injury.
Anatomy and Biomechanics

Osteology
Distal humerus, proximal ulna, and radial head make up the elbow joint
Vascular Anatomy
Brachial artery crosses the elbow joint and rarely is injured
Nerves
Median, ulnar, and radial nerves cross the elbow joint. Ulnar nerve palsies are the most
commonly reported associated nerve injury.
Joints and Ligaments
The stability of the elbow joint is provided by static and dynamic constraints (Figure 1).
Primary static constraints
Ulnohumeral articulation
Anterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament (MCL)
Lateral collateral ligament (LCL) complex, including the lateral ulnar collateral ligament
(LUCL)
Secondary static constraints
Capsule (most stabilizing effect with elbow extended)
Radiocapitellar articulation (important secondary valgus stabilizer)
Common flexor and extensor tendon origins
Dynamic constraints
Dynamic constraint is provided by the muscles that cross the elbow joint (the biceps,
triceps, and brachialis).
These muscles apply compressive force.
The MCL becomes the primary constraint to valgus instability if the radial head is resected.
Injuries to the MCL in isolation typically are well tolerated, except in overhead throwing
athletes.
The coronoid blocks rotational instability and posterior subluxation of the ulna from the
posterior pull of the triceps or if weight bearing on the hand.
50% of the coronoid height is necessary to provide substantial stability.

Sagittal plane fractures of the coronoid may disrupt the MCL insertion or cause substantial
articular deformity.
The LCL—the LUCL and the radial collateral ligament—prevent rotational subluxation of the
forearm away from the humerus. The LUCL and radial collateral ligament share a common
humeral attachment and are frequently injured in combination.
The radial head plays a minor role in posterolateral rotatory stability by tensioning the
LUCL.
Figure 1 Illustration shows how the static constraints in the elbow are analogous to the defenses
of a fortress. The primary static constraints to elbow instability are the ulnohumeral articulation,
the anterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament (MCL), and the lateral collateral ligament
(LCL) complex, including the lateral ulnar collateral ligament. The secondary constraints include
the capsule, the radiocapitellar articulation, and the common flexor and extensor tendon origins.
(Adapted with permission from the Mayo Foundation for Medical Education and Research,
Rochester, MN.)


Anatomy and Biomechanics
The elbow joint is a complex articulation of the distal humerus, proximal radius, and
proximal ulna. Flexion and extension occur primarily through the ulnohumeral joint,
whereas pronation and supination occur through the radiohumeral articulation and the
proximal radioulnar joint. In addition to the osseous anatomy, soft-tissue structures,
including ligaments and muscles, provide stability to the joint. The neurovascular
anatomy is notable for the brachial artery, which crosses anterior to the elbow joint, and
the ulnar, radial, and median nerves.
Stability of the joint is afforded by the primary static constraints, secondary static
constraints, and dynamic constraints. The primary restraints include the ulnohumeral
articulation, anterior bundle of the MCL, and LCL complex. The congruency of the
ulnohumeral articulation imparts stability in the coronal and sagittal planes. The distal
olecranon imparts varus/valgus stability through the greater sigmoid notch with the
elbow fully extended, whereas the coronoid provides anterior/posterior stability. The
secondary static constraints include the capsule, radiocapitellar articulation, and
common flexor and extensor origins. The dynamic constraints, although perhaps less
important than the bony and ligamentous restraints, include the brachialis and triceps,
which generate compressive forces across the elbow to increase joint stability. All of
these bony, ligamentous, and muscular stabilizers act in concert to render the elbow a
stable joint.
The MCL consists of the anterior bundle, posterior bundle, and transverse bundle. The
anterior band imparts restraint against valgus force. Biomechanical studies have noted
the anterior band to be the primary restraint to valgus force during flexion range of
motion.3,4 The anterior bundle, which runs from the medial epicondyle to the sublime
tubercle, has an anterior band that is taut from 0° to 60° and a posterior band that is
taut from 90° to 120° of flexion, allowing for stability throughout range of motion.3 A
portion of the anterior bundle is isometric throughout the arc of flexion, which explains
its function as a primary static constraint.5 The posterior and transverse bundles play
little role in coronal plane stability.6
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:09 AM
AAOS | Acute and Recurrent Elbow Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
5/33

The MCL has particular importance in overhead throwing athletes who rely on valgus
stability throughout throwing motion. Isolated injuries to the MCL are otherwise well
tolerated. The radiocapitellar articulation is the secondary stabilizer to valgus and most
commonly is disrupted in patients with a radial head fracture. Morrey and An7
demonstrated this in a cadaveric model by differentially removing the radial head, MCL,
or both. Radial head resection in isolation did not impart valgus instability because the
MCL provided primary restraint; however, MCL resection with an intact radial head
resulted in valgus instability.7 These two structures must be evaluated together to
appropriately manage valgus instability.
The LCL complex consists of the LUCL, annular ligament, accessory LCL, and radial
collateral ligament.8 This complex is responsible for preventing rotational subluxation of
the forearm from the distal humerus. O’Driscoll et al9 were the first to demonstrate the
important role the LCL complex plays in posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI). The
authors found that as the radial head dislocates away from the humerus, the LUCL is
compromised while the annular ligament remains intact.9
The anterior capsule and coronoid are important structures for maintaining stability with
the elbow in extension. These structures counteract the posterior pull of the triceps to
prevent posterior dislocation.
Etiology
Mechanisms of injury for posterolateral dislocations
The classic mechanism of injury is thought to be a combination of axial load, external
rotation of the forearm (supination), and valgus force (valgus posterolateral). A progressive
circular disruption of the soft tissues occurs beginning on the lateral side of the elbow (Table
1).
Posterolateral elbow dislocation also may occur via a combination of axial load, external
rotation of the forearm, and varus force.
The LCL complex is disrupted with all elbow dislocations. Some studies believe that the MCL
is always disrupted with elbow dislocation; however, this is controversial.

Table 1 Stages of Soft-Tissue Disruption
Stage
Description
1
Disruption of the LUCL
2
Disruption of the other lateral ligamentous structures and the anterior and posterior
capsules
3
Disruption of the MCL
3A
Partial disruption of the MCL
3B
Complete disruption of the MCL
3C
Distal humerus stripped of soft tissues; severe instability results in dislocation or
subluxation
LUCL = lateral ulnar collateral ligament, MCL = medial collateral ligament.
Adapted from O’Driscoll SW: Acute, recurrent, and chronic elbow instabilities, in Norris TR, ed:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Shoulder and Elbow, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2002, pp 313-323.
Valgus instability
Mechanism and pattern of injury—acute valgus instability in non-throwers
Valgus instability also can occur after a fall on an outstretched hand and a direct valgus
load.
Injury to the anterior band of the MCL is the essential lesion.
PLRI
PLRI may occur after elbow dislocation, iatrogenically, or in a delayed fashion after varus
malunion of the distal humerus.
Insufficiency of the LUCL is the essential lesion.
Deficiencies in the coronoid, radial head, and MCL may further destabilize the elbow in a
rotational manner.
A fall onto an outstretched hand that supinates the forearm with a valgus thrust and axially
loads the forearm leads to PLRI.
PLRI is primarily an instability pattern of the ulnohumeral articulation, with secondary
involvement of the radiocapitellar joint.
The radioulnar articulation remains stable.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
7/33

The elbow dislocates as a result of progressive failure of the LCL (radial collateral ligament
and LUCL); the anterior capsule; and, possibly, the MCL (Figure 2). In many patients, the
common extensor origin is avulsed proximally from the lateral epicondyle.
In a small number of patients, an elbow dislocation will lead to recurrent PLRI of the elbow.
Most patients are successfully treated via brief immobilization and early protected range of
motion.
Tardy posterolateral elbow instability is a potential late complication of a varus
supracondylar humerus malunion, which may result in LCL attritional failure.
In tardy posterolateral elbow instability, the abnormal lateral thrust across the joint line
caused by the malunion slowly stretches the LUCL over time.

Figure 2 Illustration of an elbow shows how excessive rotation of the forearm leads to
progressive disruption of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL), which may propagate to
include the anterior capsule and the medial collateral ligament (MCL). (Reproduced from
Updegrove GF, Getz CL: Acute and recurrent elbow instability, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 824-831.)
Varus posteromedial instability (VPMI)
Mechanism and pattern of injury
VPMI may occur after a fall on an outstretched hand that applies a varus thrust to the
elbow.
A combined sagittal coronoid fracture and an LUCL injury are the essential lesions.
The instability occurs as the distal humerus subluxates into the proximal ulnar lesion. If this
occurs, the proximal ulna rotates in a posterior and varus direction, producing
incongruency.
On the lateral aspect of the elbow, traction tears of the lateral ligaments occur, usually
without bony injury.

Etiology
The classic pathoanatomy of a posterolateral elbow dislocation was described by
O’Driscoll et al10 and was termed the Horii circle. The Horii circle describes the energy
that travels around the elbow through three stages. Stage 1 is on the lateral side of the
elbow with disruption of the LUCL. Stage 2 involves anterior and posterior soft-tissue
disruptions, leading to posterolateral dislocation of the elbow. Stage 3 involves
disruption around to the medial structures. Stage 3A involves disruption of the posterior
band of the MCL, stage 3B involves disruption of the entire MCL, and stage 3C includes
disruption of the flexor-pronator origin and all soft-tissue attachments of the distal
humerus. Other studies have challenged whether a posterolateral dislocation is possible
with an intact MCL based on experimental models.10,11
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:09 AM
AAOS | Acute and Recurrent Elbow Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
10/33

Valgus instability, although most classically occurring in throwers, also can result from
trauma. The proposed mechanism of injury is valgus and external rotation to a slightly
flexed elbow. In a study in which this force was applied to a cadaver model specimen, 8
of 10 cadaver model specimens sustained lesions to the MCL.12 Therefore, the essential
lesion is to the MCL, with the anterior band most commonly involved.
PLRI is another type of instability that often occurs after trauma.13 The mechanism of
injury tends to be a valgus force with the forearm supinated.10 PLRI was initially
described by O’Driscoll et al9 in 1991, with the primary lesion to the LUCL. The annular
ligament is intact, which maintains the proximal radioulnar joint. As the forearm
progresses into supination, the radial head dislocates posteriorly because of the
incompetent LUCL complex. Most patients can be treated via a brief period of
immobilization and rehabilitation. In rare patients, the entire LCL complex and the lateral
capsule are pulled off the humeral epicondyle.14 These lesions may lead to chronic
instability. Such patients benefit from surgical reconstruction of the LUCL. Distal
humerus varus malunions also may lead to PLRI via gradual stretching of the LUCL.
Management of this tardy instability involves osteotomy and ligament reconstruction.
VPMI differs from PLRI in that a coronoid fracture accompanies the LUCL lesion. This
occurs after a fall onto an outstretched hand with a varus force. The distal humerus
subluxes into the coronoid fracture, rendering the joint unstable in the coronal plane. In
this injury pattern, the radial head is not fractured as it is in patients with a terrible triad
injury.
Classification
Acute Dislocation
Elbow dislocations are classified according to whether they are simple or complex and the
direction of displacement.
Simple versus complex dislocation
Simple: dislocation without osseous injury
SEND FEEDBACK

11/33

Complex: dislocation with osseous injury
Terrible triad injury: characterized by an elbow dislocation with an LCL complex tear, a
radial head fracture, and a coronoid fracture
Varus posteromedial rotatory instability: characterized by an LCL tear with a fracture of the
medial facet of the coronoid or a comminuted coronoid fracture
Direction of displacement (position of the distal fragment relative to the proximal fragment)
Posterior dislocations are most common. They can be:
Posterior
Posterolateral
Posteromedial (Figure 3)
Anterior, medial, lateral, and divergent dislocations also can occur but are rare.


Classification
Classification of injuries is based upon the presence or absence of a fracture. Simple
dislocations are purely soft-tissue injuries, whereas complex dislocations are associated
with fractures. The two most common complex dislocations are terrible triad injury and
varus posteromedial rotatory instability. Terrible triad injury involves a LCL complex tear,
radial head fracture, and coronoid fracture. Dislocations are described by the position of
the distal fragment (ulna/radius) relative to the proximal fragment (humerus). Although
posterior dislocations are the most common, any direction of dislocation can occur.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Fall onto an outstretched hand, immediate deformity of the elbow
Physical Examination
Acute Dislocation
Neurovascular status should be documented (before and after elbow reduction).
Open injuries and compartment syndrome, which require immediate surgical management,
should be ruled out.
Valgus Instability
Findings associated with acute valgus instability include tenderness to palpation along the MCL
and medial elbow bruising and swelling.
Ulnar nerve irritation at the cubital tunnel may result from stretching of the nerve in the
unstable elbow.
Rupture of the flexor-pronator group may occur from traumatic valgus load to the elbow.
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:09 AM
AAOS | Acute and Recurrent Elbow Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
14/33

Physical examination tests attempt to re-create the mechanism of injury of forearm supination
and axial load.
The most common physical examination tests performed to detect PLRI are the PLRI stress
test, the posterior drawer test, the table-top relocation test, the push-up test, and the chair-
rise test.
Varus Posteromedial Instability
Physical examination—Decreased range of motion; painful arc of motion; and, occasionally,
crepitus are noted.

Physical Examination
The history of a patient with an acute dislocation often involves a fall onto an
outstretched hand. The patient will report immediate deformity of the elbow. With
chronic instability, the patient often will describe a shifting sensation and weakness.
The physical examination of a patient with an acute dislocation begins with assessing the
soft tissues and neurovascular status. Rarely, dislocations can be open, which is an
indication for surgical irrigation and débridement. Neurovascular examination involves
assessing radial, median, and ulnar nerve distributions. The posterior and anterior
interosseous nerves should be evaluated for motor function. The neurovascular
examination should be documented before reduction and immediately after reduction.
Radial and ulnar pulses also should be assessed.
The forearm compartment should be assessed to evaluate for compartment syndrome.
This is more common in patients with a dislocation associated with a crushing
mechanism of injury or a vascular injury. If concern for compartment syndrome exists,
then the clinician should evaluate for early findings of compartment syndrome, which
include pain out of proportion to the physical examination, pain with passive flexion and
extension of the digits, and paresthesias. If clinical concern for compartment syndrome
exists, then immediate fasciotomies should be performed.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:09 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
15/33

Acute valgus instability may occur in patients with trauma or in overhead throwing
athletes. These athletes often will describe a pop or acute medial pain with a particular
throw. On physical examination, pain often is medial along the MCL. Ecchymosis and
swelling are not uncommon. This patient will have valgus instability on physical
examination. Careful ulnar nerve examination is critical because patients with chronic
valgus instability, particularly overhead throwing athletes, may have irritation of the
ulnar nerve. If surgical management is indicated, the ulnar nerve often is subsequently
addressed via decompression or transposition. The flexor-pronator mass should be
tested and palpated because this also may be detached at the time of injury.
PLRI often occurs because of insufficiency of the LUCL after a traumatic dislocation.
Many patients will note mechanical symptoms and pain with elbow extension or when
pushing up from a chair. This type of instability often occurs with axial load, valgus, and
forearm supination, which compromises the lateral complex and forces the radial head
posterior. The physical examination maneuvers to test for PLRI involve re-creating this
mechanism of injury to test for subjective or objective instability. Patients often will have
tenderness to palpation of the LUCL, varus instability, and positive provocative tests.
These tests include the lateral pivot-shift test, the posterior drawer test, the table-top
relocation test, and the chair-rise test.
LUCL and coronoid anteromedial facet fracture are the essential lesions associated with
VPMI. These patients tend to present with lack of range of motion and crepitus because
of coronoid fracture. If patients can tolerate ligamentous testing, they will have
substantial varus laxity with the elbow in extension and slight flexion.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Acute Dislocation
Plain AP and lateral radiographs of the elbow are necessary to document congruent reduction.
Oblique views may be useful to identify periarticular fractures.
Valgus Instability
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:09 AM
AAOS | Acute and Recurrent Elbow Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
16/33

Radiographs typically are normal with valgus instability. In skeletally immature patients, injury
to the medial epicondyle physis may be observed.
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
In purely ligamentous PLRI, radiographs will be normal; however, associated lesions of the
radial head, capitellum, coronoid, and articular surface may be observed.
Varus Posteromedial Instability
With VPMI, AP radiographs will demonstrate a loss of articular congruency of the medial joint
line and/or a sagittal coronoid fracture. Opening of the radiocapitellar articulation is common,
indicating injury to the lateral ligaments.
Radial head fractures are not observed with this injury pattern. This distinguishes VPMI from a
terrible triad injury.

Radiography
The initial imaging modality is plain radiographs. AP and lateral radiographs are best to
assess for dislocation. Post-reduction, the joint line must be carefully examined for
subtle incongruences or incarcerated fragments. Oblique radiographs also can be
obtained to assess for fracture.
The medial epicondyle often may be fractured in skeletally immature patients with
valgus instability. Careful assessment of these structures is important. Similarly, if a frank
dislocation exists, then the medial epicondyle may be incarcerated in the joint after
reduction. Careful assessment of a good lateral radiograph is imperative.
In patients with purely ligamentous forms of instability, radiographs often are normal.
However, the clinician must be aware of typical fracture patterns associated with elbow
instability. Terrible triad injury involves fractures of the radial head and the coronoid.
Conversely, VPMI often involves anteromedial facet fractures of the coronoid without
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:09 AM
AAOS | Acute and Recurrent Elbow Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
17/33

fracture of the radial head. This type of instability may be associated with widening of
the radiocapitellar articulation, indicating varus drift.
Computed Tomography
Acute Dislocation
CT is useful to identify associated osseous injury.
With an incongruous reduction, CT or MRI should be considered to identify potential
incarcerated osteocartilaginous fragments.
Valgus Instability
CT may be obtained in patients with a medial fracture, especially if concern for displacement
or an incarcerated fragment exists.
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
CT is helpful to evaluate for associated bony injury.
Varus Posteromedial Instability
CT is the best imaging study to define the orientation and size of the coronoid fracture (Figure
4).

arrow indicates the fracture fragment. (Reproduced from Steinmann SP: Coronoid process
fractures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2008;16[9]:519-529.)

Computed Tomography
A CT scan can be obtained to assess for osseous injury and better understand the
fracture characteristics. CT may be particularly helpful in planning surgical fixation of the
fracture, such as fracture of the coronoid. If available, three-dimensional CT
reconstruction is recommended because the complex orientation of the elbow may
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:09 AM
AAOS | Acute and Recurrent Elbow Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
19/33

make it difficult to obtain CT cuts in the appropriate plane. CT also is useful to identify
incarcerated fragments.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Acute Dislocation
With an incongruous reduction, CT or MRI should be considered to identify potential
incarcerated osteocartilaginous fragments.
Valgus Instability
MRI is not necessary but may confirm the diagnosis and assess the integrity of the
flexor/pronator muscle/tendon.
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
MRI is unreliable for assessing the integrity of the LUCL because of the oblique course of the
ligament. Posterior subluxation of the radial head in extension and a bald epicondyle may be
suggestive. Cartilaginous injury may be appreciated on magnetic resonance arthrograms.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is best used to assess the integrity of the ligamentous structures and cartilage. If
joint incongruency is observed on radiographs, MRI is useful in identifying incarcerated
fragments, particularly in younger patients because the fragments may be mostly
cartilaginous. In patients with a ligamentous or osteochondral injury, a magnetic
resonance arthrogram may be useful to increase the sensitivity. In patients with valgus
instability, MRIs will reveal MCL injury and possible injury to the flexor/pronator origin on
the medial epicondyle. In patients with PLRI, injury to the LUCL often is observed on MRI;
however, the oblique course of the LUCL may be difficult to see on MRI and an injury
may be missed. Stress radiographs and examination under anesthesia may be necessary
in difficult-to-determine cases.

9/3/26, 7:09 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
20/33

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Acute Dislocation
An algorithm for the management of simple elbow dislocations is shown in Figure 5.
Reduction of the joint under adequate analgesia is performed first. For posterior dislocations,
controlled reduction is performed by applying inline traction, progressive elbow flexion, and
anterior-directed force to the olecranon.
Post-reduction stability is assessed. In posterior dislocations, the elbow typically is more
unstable in extension. The degree of instability should be noted because this may be useful in
determining how far to extend the elbow during physical therapy. If the elbow re-dislocates
before 30° of flexion, early ligament repair may be necessary. Therefore, the elbow should be
immobilized in 90° of flexion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:09 AM
AAOS | Acute and Recurrent Elbow Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
21/33

Figure 5 Algorithm for the management of a simple elbow dislocation. LCL = lateral collateral
ligament, MCL = medial collateral ligament. (Adapted from Armstrong AD: Acute, recurrent, and
chronic elbow instability, in Galatz LM, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Shoulder and Elbow, ed
3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2008, pp 461-476.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:09 AM
AAOS | Acute and Recurrent Elbow Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001065
22/33

If the LCL is disrupted and the MCL is intact, then the elbow will be more stable with the
forearm in pronation.
If the LCL and the MCL are disrupted, the forearm should be immobilized in neutral (Figure 6).
A posterior splint is applied. Typically, the forearm is placed in a splint for 5 to 7 days, with the
elbow positioned at 90° and with appropriate forearm rotation.
Post-reduction radiographic assessment (AP and lateral views with the elbow at 90° and with
appropriate forearm rotation) is performed to confirm concentric reduction. Attention is
directed to ensuring concentric ulnohumeral reduction and alignment of the radial head with
the capitellum. After reduction is confirmed, the arm is immobilized for 5 to 7 days. Depending
on stability, the splint can be removed to allow for early, active range-of-motion exercises
using a brace with or without an extension block.
Figure 6 Radiographs of the elbow of a patient who sustained a direct lateral elbow dislocation.
Post-reduction lateral (A) and AP (B) radiographs obtained with the forearm in pronation. Note
the incongruency of the ulnohumeral joint on the lateral view and the medial gapping on the AP
view. The splint was changed, and lateral (C) and AP (D) radiographs were obtained with the
forearm in neutral, allowing for congruent reduction of the elbow joint. The forearm position in
pronation accentuated a medial-sided injury, whereas neutral forearm rotation allowed for
concentric reduction by off-loading the medial- and lateral-sided soft-tissue injuries. (Reproduced
from Updegrove GF, Getz CL: Acute and recurrent elbow instability, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 824-831.)

Acute Dislocation
Initial management of acute dislocations involves urgent reduction of the joint. This can
be achieved with the use of sedative medications and analgesia. Manipulation usually

involves traction and flexion. Physical examination of the elbow after reduction should
be performed to determine ligamentous injury. A brief period of immobilization in a
posterior long arm splint with the elbow in 90° of flexion is necessary. If the MCL is
intact, typically the forearm is immobilized in pronation. If the MCL is disrupted, the
elbow should be immobilized in neutral rotation. Adequate post-reduction radiographs
are necessary to confirm reduction. Advanced imaging studies, including CT and MRI, can
be obtained to evaluate complex fractures or assess for incarcerated fragments at the
discretion of the clinician.
Although evidence shows that immobilization for more than 2 to 3 weeks may result in
long-term loss of elbow motion,15,16 more recent studies have compared functional
motion with immobilization. The FuncSiE (functional treatment versus plaster for simple
elbow dislocations) trial was published by Iordens et al17 in 2017. This multicenter trial
randomized 100 patients with a simple elbow dislocation to 3 weeks of plaster
immobilization or a soft wrap with range of motion exercises beginning 2 days
postinjury. The early motion group had better range of motion at 6 weeks postinjury;
however, no differences were noted between the two groups at 1 year postinjury. The
functional range of motion group also returned to work sooner; however, no difference
in any functional outcome measures, secondary surgeries, or complications were noted
between the two groups at 1 year postinjury.
Early range of motion and rehabilitation is necessary to achieve a good outcome.
Depending on the patient, this can be achieved via a therapist-directed protocol or home
exercise program.
Valgus Instability
Traumatic ruptures typically are managed via a period of immobilization and early physical
therapy.
During the early mobilization period, valgus stress must be avoided.
A small number of patients with traumatic valgus instability will experience recurrent
instability.
Surgical indications

Medial physeal fracture: the presence of an incarcerated fragment or displacement of the
fragment more than 5 mm (relative indication)
Skeletally mature: high-demand athlete or severe displacement of flexor/pronator tendon
(relative indications)
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
Avoiding provocative positions, brace management, and strengthening of the extensors may
decrease symptoms in milder cases.

Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
Patients with evidence of valgus instability and PLRI should be treated via early
functional rehabilitation. Strengthening of the flexor-pronator mass in patients with
valgus instability and the common extensors in patients with PLRI are key components
of rehabilitation. In each patient, provocative maneuvers should be avoided to limit
stress on the injured ligaments. Most of these patients have good outcomes with
nonsurgical treatment. Surgical treatment is reserved for high-level throwing athletes
with valgus instability. Skeletally immature patients with incarcerated fragments also
should be treated surgically.
Surgical Management
Indications/Contraindications
Acute Dislocation
Stability of the elbow cannot be achieved via reduction and immobilization.
Osteochondral fragment or soft-tissue entrapment prevents concentric reduction.
Complex dislocation with associated fractures
Open injuries
Neurovascular injuries requiring surgical management
Relative indication: reducible joint that is unstable (dislocates) with the elbow extended
between 90° and 60°
Contraindications: patients with severe medical comorbidities

Indications/Contraindications
The absolute indications for surgical management include inability to maintain a reduced
elbow joint, entrapped soft tissue or osteochondral fragment, fractures associated with
dislocation, open injuries, or neurovascular injuries that require surgical repair. In
patients with inability to maintain reduction, acute ligamentous repair or external
fixation should be considered. Entrapped fragments should be removed from the joint
to allow for concentric reduction. Open reduction and internal fixation is indicated for
coronoid fractures, radial head fractures (versus radial head replacement), and displaced
epicondyle fractures. Surgical treatment should be considered in patients with a
reducible joint and instability between 60° and 90° given the high risk of re-dislocation.
Techniques/Procedures 
Acute dislocation
Surgical procedures
The incision can be made in the posterior midline or on the lateral elbow over the Kocher
interval (extensor carpi ulnaris and anconeus) with or without a medial approach.
Open reduction of the elbow with repair (or reconstruction) of the LCL complex is
performed; then stability is assessed.
If the elbow is still unstable, then the MCL is repaired (or reconstructed); then stability is
reassessed.
Hinged or static external fixation is required only if the elbow is unstable after other
surgical procedures result in failure to maintain a concentric, stable reduction.
PLRI
For grossly unstable elbows and elbows in which nonsurgical management fails, LUCL
reconstruction with the use of a graft is indicated.
Graft material may be autograft or allograft. Palmaris longus, plantaris, gracilis, lateral triceps
fascia, or other common tendon graft material may be used.
VPMI
Early recognition of the instability pattern and management is necessary to avoid rapid onset
of posttraumatic arthritis.

Management of VPMI consists of repair of the LCL and restoration of the proximal ulnar joint
surface and/or open reduction and internal fixation of the coronoid fracture.
Anteromedial coronoid fractures that are small, minimally displaced, and demonstrate no
evidence of elbow subluxation may be managed nonsurgically.
Outcomes are improved with anatomic reduction and secure coronoid fixation. Varus
malalignment of the anteromedial facet or varus subluxation of the elbow may lead to
arthritic changes and poor functional results.

Surgical Management 
Surgical management of acute dislocations is rare. Approximately 2.3% of patients with a
simple elbow dislocation require surgical stabilization procedures.18 The decision to
perform acute ligament repair or reconstruction depends on the degree of soft-tissue
injury and associated instability. Based upon the Horii circle, the lateral complex is
always injured, and, therefore, should be addressed first. The Kocher interval between
the extensor carpi ulnaris and the anconeus is developed, and the LCL complex is
evaluated. Repair of the LCL complex is performed. Reconstruction may be considered if
the tissue quality is very poor or unable to mobilize to the anatomic footprint. After
completion of the lateral repair, the elbow should be reassessed for stability. If it
remains unstable, a medial incision should be made to address the MCL. Careful
dissection around the ulnar nerve is necessary. The MCL can then be repaired or
reconstructed, depending on the tissue quality and degree of injury. If the elbow
remains unstable after addressing the medial and lateral ligamentous complexes, then
an external fixator should be added to maintain reduction.
PLRI involves injury to the LCL complex, and, therefore, this is the structure addressed
surgically. Open and arthroscopic techniques have been described, each of which is
associated with satisfactory results.19 In patients with acute instability, the LUCL can be
repaired, whereas reconstruction is indicated for revision procedures. Various graft
options are available, with palmaris longus autograft being the most popular. Various
techniques have been described for reconstruction. Nestor et al20 described a
transosseous tunnel and overlay graft technique. The suture is passed through the

which the graft is secured by sutures tied over a bony bridge.
VPMI is quite rare but often is managed surgically to prevent posttraumatic arthritis. A
recent series of 27 patients treated surgically was reported, with all patients requiring
LCL repair and open reduction and internal fixation of the coranoid.22 Although this
often can be accomplished via a lateral Kocher interval, occasionally a medial approach
is necessary to fix the coronoid fracture with the use of a buttress plate.23 In rare
patients, if the coronoid fracture is small and nondisplaced, it can be managed
nonsurgically. Poor reduction or displacement of the coronoid may lead to varus
subluxation and posttraumatic arthritis.
Postoperative Management
Acute dislocation
Rehabilitation—Depending on the postoperative stability of the elbow, active range of
motion exercises may be initiated with the use of a brace with or without an extension block.
The extension block may be decreased gradually or removed at approximately 2 to 3 weeks
for a goal of full active extension approximately 6 to 8 weeks postinjury. Active range of
motion exercises are performed through the stable arc, maintaining the most stable position
of the forearm throughout the arc of motion. Active pronation and supination with the elbow
at 90° are initiated as soon as the splint is removed (5 to 7 days postinjury) to prevent
rotational contracture.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Acute dislocation
Pearls and pitfalls
The most common pitfall is failure to attain and maintain concentric reduction after
surgical or nonsurgical management. The joint must be reduced concentrically, and
management does not stop until satisfactory reduction is achieved.
Forearm rotation is used to its fullest advantage to attain or maintain concentric reduction.
Early, active range of motion through a stable arc with the use of splints may help prevent
contracture.

If open reduction is required, a stepwise surgical approach should be followed.

Postoperative Management
The postoperative course should involve early, aggressive range of motion initiated
within the first few weeks. Various motion protocols have been developed to maintain
functional motion.23,24 A recent protocol involves overhead motion and allows for
maintained stability of the joint through the arc of motion.23 This has been shown to
minimize the effects of gravity and allow the triceps to act as a joint stabilizer.25 Based
on the type of instability and clinical examination, forearm rotation should be used (such
as maximal pronation or supination) to enhance stability during rehabilitation. The goal
of rehabilitation is to fully restore motion by 6 to 8 weeks postinjury. Early forearm
rotation is initiated immediately during the rehabilitation process to prevent a rotational
contracture. The clinician must balance joint stability with early functional motion to
achieve a satisfactory outcome.
Complications
Acute Dislocation
Loss of extension (most common)
Early, active range of motion exercises may help prevent or minimize occurrence.
Static, progressive splinting may be initiated if the elbow is less inflamed (typically, 6 to 8
weeks postinjury).
Neurovascular injuries
Compartment syndrome
Articular surface injuries
Chronic or recurrent elbow instability. Residual laxity is commonly observed on stress
radiographs; however, recurrent instability is observed in less than 10% to 20% of patients.
Late osteoarthritis
Heterotopic ossification

Complications
The most common complication after an acute dislocation is stiffness. Approximately
1.2% of patients require contracture releases after a simple elbow dislocation.18 To
avoid this complication, early motion should be initiated and static, progressive splinting
should be initiated at approximately 6 weeks postinjury for at-risk patients. Recurrent or
late instability is rare after an acute dislocation but should be addressed via
reconstruction of the affected ligaments. Heterotopic ossification has been reported and
is more common in polytrauma patients and patients with head injuries. Late
osteoarthritis is a rare complication but is more common in patients with VPMI. Lastly, a
good initial physical examination is necessary to avoid complications such as
compartment syndrome or missed neurovascular injury.
